comments.author: @OkaySheepGuy
comments.text:
> we don't know the origin of Basque, ooooo spooky!

But we do, at-least with moderate confidence. The Basque have a higher percentage of Western Hunter-Gatherer ancestry, and their language is evidently paleoeuropean. It's not related to Etruscan or Minoan, two languages which are assumed to be Anatolian in origin, nor is it related to other families. 

The evidence generally points to Basque being descended from whatever language the Western Hunter-Gatherer who inhabited Iberia spoke before Anatolian and Steppe Eurasian immigration.

comments.author: @ambergris5705
comments.text: I feel like omitting arpitan (franco-provençal) is doing it a disservice. The name franco-provençal itself is a disservice as it's neither a French language nor a provençal one (even though it has similar substrate to both), but it definitely is its own thing, that was spoken beyond the borders into Switzerland and (still today) in Italy. It used to be spoken in really important cities like Lyon, Saint-Étienne, Geneva, Lausanne, etc. It's often forgotten, because it has disappeared a lot more than other local languages, and its cross border nature didn't help coordination (although it help to protect it in a weird roundabout way).

comments.author: @aaronmarks9366
comments.text: There's another Romance language that is on the map but wasn't described: Franco-Provençal, spoken in the areas of the French Alps, Savoy, and into western Switzerland and northwestern Italy (Aosta region). It is the original "French" of Suisse Romande and the surrounding area, and has features that are similar to both Langues d'Oïl and Langues d'Oc, but it is it's own Romance variety.
